title: Solana network came within minutes of full freeze after routing glitch knocked out 28% of stake
dek: A routing failure at a single Miami data center took 28.83% of Solana's staked tokens offline on Wednesday, bringing the network within 20 million tokens of triggering a finality halt that would freeze all transactions. The incident exposed concentration risk, with one network operator (AS2032) controlling more than a quarter of all staked tokens.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: A routing glitch at Teraswitch's Miami facility knocked offline 28.83% of Solana's staked tokens, placing the network within 86% of the 33% finality-halt threshold before the issue was resolved in approximately 10 minutes.
bottom_line: Solana is watching the fallout from the incident, with the network and its validators assessing whether backup systems and operator concentration limits will change. To watch: whether Solana implements new limits on stake concentration for single operators or mandates geographic diversification of infrastructure, and whether validators adopt working failover systems. The incident would be invalidated if network operators voluntarily redistributed stake below the one-third threshold and if Teraswitch's Miami facility routing issues are not repeated.
body: A routing failure at Teraswitch's Miami data center knocked 28.83 percent of Solana's staked tokens offline on Wednesday morning, according to reporting from CoinDesk, bringing the network within 20 million tokens of the threshold required to trigger a complete finality halt. The network stops finalizing transactions if more than one-third of all staked tokens go offline. The outage, reported by Marinade Finance, reveals a critical vulnerability: one single network operator, identified as AS2032, controlled more than a quarter of all the tokens people had staked to secure the network, exceeding Solana's own prescribed safety limits for concentration. Nearly all tokens controlled by AS2032 went offline at the same time, according to CoinDesk. Other companies lost another 14 million tokens in the same period.

The routing glitch originated at the Miami facility but spread across multiple continents. The bad internet route cut off validators in London, Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Singapore and Tokyo. North America validators stayed online during the incident. Teraswitch fixed the issue in about 10 minutes, and traffic was flowing again by 4:16 a.m. UTC, per CoinDesk's reporting.

Most affected validators, including the major operator Helius, stayed offline for the full 33 minutes because their backup systems never switched on, according to CoinDesk. This shows insufficient failover mechanisms among network participants. Roughly 90 validators were hit and together lost 333 SOL in rewards, a relatively small sum that will be covered by validator bonds.

The consequences of a full finality halt would have been far more severe. A finality halt in February 2024 took about five hours to restart. If Wednesday's outage had crossed the one-third threshold, all SOL holders would have faced a frozen network with no clear recovery bond available. Solana has $4.3 billion locked in DeFi protocols operating on the network, all of which would have been rendered inaccessible during a halt.

Solana has faced several outages in the past, according to CoinDesk. The network has built a reputation as a faster and cheaper alternative to Ethereum, but this incident underscores the tension between the network's performance gains and its concentration of stake in single operators and shared infrastructure dependencies.

The incident exposes two layers of risk: the structural reliance on a single network operator controlling more than the safety-prescribed share of stake, and the physical dependency on infrastructure controlled by a single ISP. A routing glitch at one facility cascaded across continents, demonstrating how localized infrastructure failures can have global impact on validator connectivity. The network came within 86 percent of the finality-halt threshold, leaving a dangerously narrow safety margin between normal operation and full network freeze.
